grandiose

GRAN-dee-ohss -- from Latin grandis, 'big, great,' plus -ose, 'full of': full of grandness, and then some. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Grandiose is excessively grand, inflated far beyond what the situation can support.

The developer's grandiose vision called for a ski slope in the middle of the desert.

Worked Example

A first-year club president announces that the chess team, which has four members and one battered board, will host an international tournament with a live orchestra by December.

A plan far grander than the situation could possibly support is exactly what grandiose describes. Unlike 'ambitious,' which can be admirable, grandiose hints that the whole thing is too big and too showy to be real.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pompous: Pompous describes a person puffed up with self-importance -- a pompous speaker, a pompous official. Grandiose usually judges plans and schemes instead: it says the project itself is far grander than reality can support, not that its maker talks down to people.

showy: Showy means designed to attract attention, and a showy thing can still be exactly the right size for its job. Grandiose adds a failure of judgment: a grandiose plan is inflated far beyond what the situation deserves or what the planner can deliver.

extravagant: Extravagant is about excess of money and luxury -- gold fixtures, runaway spending. Grandiose is about excess of scale and claim: a plan can be grandiose on a tiny budget, promising wonders it cannot deliver, while an extravagant one simply costs far more than it should.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

modest: limited in size or claim

humble: not proud or boastful

Where it sits · how far the show outruns reality — ambitious → grandiose → fantastical

ambitious vs. grandiose: Ambitious is the neutral, often admiring version of grandiose -- an ambitious plan is merely bold, while a grandiose plan is so oversized that people start to doubt it.

fantastical vs. grandiose: Fantastical goes past grandiose into pure make-believe: a grandiose plan is oversized but still imaginable, while a fantastical one has left reality behind altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — grandi

Root — grandi: big, great, full-grown (from Latin grandis; the i is the linking vowel that joins the root to the suffix)

Suffix — -ose

Suffix — -ose: full of, characterized by (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Grandi ('big, great', from Latin grandis) + -ose ('full of') spell grandiose: literally 'full of grandness' -- the same root behind grand and grandeur, reaching English through Italian grandioso and French grandiose.

Use the root in a new word: grandeur

Use the root in a new word: grandeur: Nothing in the photographs prepared them for the grandeur of the canyon at sunrise.

Root Check

Word Choice

Grandiose is nearly always critical. Calling a plan 'grand' praises it; calling it 'grandiose' says it is puffed up beyond what the situation deserves or the planner can deliver.
